entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Riboflavin is vitamin B2 — a water-soluble vitamin that can also be used as a yellow food colour.
entries.expanded_summary: Riboflavin is vitamin B2 — a water-soluble vitamin that can also be used as a yellow food colour. The Schedule 8 entry also covers riboflavin-5′-phosphate sodium, a more water-soluble form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial food-grade riboflavin is commonly produced by microbial fermentation; some forms can also be made by chemical processes.
entries.fact_1_copy: This is a familiar nutrient being used for a food-technology purpose as well as having nutritional value.
entries.fact_2_copy: Riboflavin gives a yellow to yellow-orange colour.

entries.tile_summary: Ponceau 4R is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent red shade.
entries.expanded_summary: Ponceau 4R is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent red shade. It is a manufactured dye rather than a colour extracted from a food or plant.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for a stable red colour in foods and drinks.

entries.tile_summary: Green S is a synthetic green food colour made to deliver a strong, consistent green shade.
entries.expanded_summary: Green S is a synthetic green food colour made to deliver a strong, consistent green shade.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to add or restore green colour.

entries.consumer_display_name: Brilliant black BN or Brilliant Black PN
entries.entry_title: Brilliant black BN or Brilliant Black PN (151)

entries.tile_summary: Brilliant Black BN is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent black to violet-black shade.
entries.expanded_summary: Brilliant Black BN is a synthetic food colour designed to give a strong, consistent black to violet-black shade. It is a manufactured dye rather than a colour extracted from a food or plant.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled chemical synthesis and purified to food-additive specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for a stable black to violet-black colour in foods and drinks.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Lycopene is the red carotenoid pigment best known from tomatoes.
entries.expanded_summary: Lycopene is the red carotenoid pigment best known from tomatoes. Food-grade lycopene can be obtained from tomato material, microbial production or other approved manufacturing routes depending on the preparation.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial lycopene may be extracted from tomatoes or produced using controlled biological or synthetic processes, then formulated for stability.
entries.fact_1_copy: Lycopene naturally gives tomatoes and some other fruits their red colour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a red to orange-red colour.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Rubixanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow-orange colouring.
entries.expanded_summary: Rubixanthin is a carotenoid-family pigment associated with yellow-orange colouring. It belongs to the same broad natural pigment family as beta-carotene and lutein.
entries.source_preparation_copy: This carotenoid occurs in natural biological sources; commercial food-colour preparations may depend on the approved source and manufacturing specification.
entries.fact_1_copy: A xanthophyll carotenoid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for yellow-orange colouring where permitted.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: That white mineral found in chalk and limestone? It's calcium carbonate — also used in foods for colour and texture.
entries.expanded_summary: Yes, it's the mineral found in chalk and limestone. In foods, calcium carbonate (170) may provide white colour, regulate acidity or help firm a product. Food-grade calcium carbonate must meet purity specifications — it isn't simply untreated quarry material.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Food-grade calcium carbonate is produced from ground limestone or by controlled precipitation. Material sold for food use must meet the applicable purity specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: A major component of limestone, chalk and many shells.
entries.fact_2_copy: A fine white powder.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Sorbic acid is the parent acid in the sorbate preservative family.
entries.expanded_summary: Sorbic acid is the parent acid in the sorbate preservative family. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial sorbic acid is manufactured by chemical synthesis and purified for food use.
entries.fact_1_copy: Sorbic acid was first identified in rowan berries, but food-grade material is generally manufactured.
entries.fact_2_copy: Helps inhibit moulds, yeasts and some bacteria.
entries.evidence_copy: An Australian total-diet study found estimated exposure to sorbates at or below 40% of the group safety limit for every age group, including high consumers. The study used older food-consumption data and is not a current market census, but it is direct Australian exposure evidence and supports a reassuring conclusion for ordinary dietary patterns.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: Australia and New Zealand food regulator: 21st Australian Total Diet Study (2005 report; current FSANZ archive)

entries.tile_summary: Potassium benzoate is the potassium salt of benzoic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium benzoate is the potassium salt of benzoic acid. It is used in food mainly for preservation rather than for flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising benzoic acid with a potassium source.
entries.fact_1_copy: One of the benzoate preservatives.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used particularly in acidic products.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium bisulphite is a sodium bisulphite form used as part of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium bisulphite is a sodium bisulphite form used as part of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by absorbing sulphur dioxide into a sodium alkali solution under controlled conditions.
entries.fact_1_copy: Part of the sulphite preservative family.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for preservation and antioxidant effects.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Natamycin is an antifungal compound made by Streptomyces bacteria.
entries.expanded_summary: Natamycin is an antifungal compound made by Streptomyces bacteria. It is used mainly to suppress moulds and yeasts on the surfaces of certain foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by microbial fermentation, then isolated and purified from the fermentation broth.
entries.fact_1_copy: Primarily yeasts and moulds rather than bacteria.
entries.fact_2_copy: Often used as a surface preservative where permitted.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium acetate or potassium diacetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium acetate or potassium diacetate is an acetate salt derived from acetic acid. It provides acetate chemistry without adding acetic acid in exactly the same form.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising acetic acid with a potassium-containing base; diacetate forms also contain associated acetic acid.
entries.fact_1_copy: Chemically related to the acid found in vinegar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the salt and food, can help regulate acidity, preserve or influence flavour.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium propionate is the sodium salt of propionic acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium propionate is the sodium salt of propionic acid. It is used mainly as a mould-inhibiting preservative.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising propionic acid with a sodium-containing base and purifying the resulting salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Commonly associated with preservation of bread and other bakery products.
entries.fact_2_copy: Releases propionate, the active acid-related preserving species, under food conditions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Ascorbic acid is vitamin C.
entries.expanded_summary: Ascorbic acid is vitamin C. The same molecule used as a nutrient can also be added for its antioxidant chemistry, helping slow oxidation and protect colour or flavour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial ascorbic acid is produced from glucose through a multi-step industrial process that commonly combines fermentation with chemical conversion and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: This is a familiar vitamin being used for a technological function as well as having nutritional value.
entries.fact_2_copy: Acts as an antioxidant and can also support flour treatment or colour stability depending on the food.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Mixed tocopherols concentrate is a vitamin-E-rich antioxidant mixture containing several naturally occurring tocopherols, commonly recovered from vegetable-oil processing streams.
entries.expanded_summary: Mixed tocopherols concentrate is a vitamin-E-rich antioxidant mixture containing several naturally occurring tocopherols, commonly recovered from vegetable-oil processing streams.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Usually concentrated and purified from deodoriser distillates or other fractions generated during vegetable-oil refining.
entries.fact_1_copy: Typically contains a mixture of alpha-, beta-, gamma- and delta-tocopherols rather than one single compound.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to slow oxidation in fats and oils.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Dodecyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid designed to work as an antioxidant in fats and oils.
entries.expanded_summary: Dodecyl gallate is an ester of gallic acid designed to work as an antioxidant in fats and oils. The dodecyl group makes the molecule more compatible with fatty ingredients than gallic acid itself.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by chemically esterifying gallic acid with the corresponding dodecyl alcohol and purifying the product.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to slow oxidative rancidity in fats and oils.
entries.fact_2_copy: Built from gallic-acid chemistry but manufactured as a more fat-soluble ester.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Lecithin helps oil and water mix — but the number 322 alone will not tell you whether it came from soy, sunflower or egg.
entries.expanded_summary: Lecithin is a mixture rich in phospholipids that help fats and water interact. Commercial lecithin is commonly recovered from oilseed processing (such as soy or sunflower) and can also come from egg. The additive number does not identify which source was used in a particular product.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Recovered and refined from phospholipid-rich biological materials such as oilseed gums or egg yolk; the exact source can vary by product.
entries.fact_1_copy: Its phospholipids make lecithin a useful emulsifier, helping ingredients such as oil and water stay mixed.
entries.fact_2_copy: The source may be soy, sunflower, egg or another approved material, so the additive number alone does not identify the crop or animal source.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Citric acid sounds like it comes from citrus — and it does occur there — but food-grade citric acid is commonly produced by fermenting sugar.
entries.expanded_summary: Citric acid occurs naturally in citrus fruits and is part of normal cellular metabolism. Its name points to citrus, but commercial food-grade citric acid is commonly produced by fermenting sugar rather than extracting it from lemons.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Typically produced by fermenting sugar solutions with selected microorganisms, then crystallising and purifying the citric acid.
entries.fact_1_copy: Found naturally in citrus fruits and many other foods.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to add tartness, control pH and bind some metal ions; it can also support antioxidant systems.
entries.fact_3_copy: Its name points to citrus, but industrial production usually starts with sugar and fermentation.

entries.consumer_display_name: Potassium tartrate or Potassium acid tartrate
entries.entry_title: Potassium tartrate or Potassium acid tartrate (336)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with an existing material — natural or manufactured — and deliberately transforms it using processes such as heating, roasting, oxidation, hydrolysis, neutralisation or other controlled treatment. The starting material can be materially changed in colour, structure or food-technology behaviour.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium tartrate / potassium acid tartrate is a potassium salt of tartaric acid, the fruit acid closely associated with grapes and wine.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium tartrate / potassium acid tartrate is a potassium salt of tartaric acid, the fruit acid closely associated with grapes and wine.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by neutralising purified tartaric acid or recovering and refining naturally formed tartrate salts from food-processing streams.
entries.fact_1_copy: Built from tartaric acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for acidity control, buffering, stabilisation or raising-agent chemistry depending on the salt.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Ammonium phosphates are a family of ammonium salts of phosphoric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium phosphates are a family of ammonium salts of phosphoric acid. Schedule 8 groups several mono-, di- or tribasic forms under the same additive number.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting purified phosphoric acid with ammonium-containing mineral or chemical bases and controlling the degree of neutralisation.
entries.fact_1_copy: Different phosphate forms have different acidity, solubility and buffering behaviour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the form, phosphates can regulate acidity, act in raising systems, stabilise texture or bind water.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Metatartaric acid is a polymerised or condensed form of tartaric acid used mainly for stabilisation rather than for adding straightforward sourness.
entries.expanded_summary: Metatartaric acid is a polymerised or condensed form of tartaric acid used mainly for stabilisation rather than for adding straightforward sourness.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by heating tartaric acid under controlled conditions so some molecules condense into larger structures.
entries.fact_1_copy: Tartaric acid, the fruit acid associated with grapes.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to help control crystal formation, particularly tartrate crystals in wine.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium fumarate is the sodium salt of fumaric acid, a strong dicarboxylic food acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium fumarate is the sodium salt of fumaric acid, a strong dicarboxylic food acid.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by neutralising purified fumaric acid with a sodium-containing base.
entries.fact_1_copy: Derived from fumaric acid chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used mainly for acidity control, buffering or related processing effects.

entries.consumer_display_name: Calcium disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetate or calcium disodium EDTA
entries.entry_title: Calcium disodium ethylenediaminetetraacetate or calcium disodium EDTA (385)
entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium disodium EDTA is a chelating agent: its molecule can bind metal ions tightly.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium disodium EDTA is a chelating agent: its molecule can bind metal ions tightly. That makes it useful for slowing metal-catalysed colour, flavour or oxidation changes in some foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by chemical synthesis of EDTA followed by conversion to the calcium disodium salt and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Binds trace metal ions that can accelerate oxidation or quality loss.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a sequestrant or stabilising agent in specified foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium alginate is the calcium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium alginate is the calcium salt of alginic acid, part of a family of gel-forming carbohydrates obtained from brown seaweed.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Brown seaweed is washed, extracted and processed to isolate alginate; the required acid or salt form is then purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Alginate is a structural polysaccharide in brown algae.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to thicken, stabilise or form gels depending on the form and food.

entries.consumer_display_name: Locust bean gum or carob bean gum
entries.entry_title: Locust bean gum or carob bean gum (410)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Locust bean gum / carob bean gum is the ground and purified galactomannan from carob seeds.
entries.expanded_summary: Locust bean gum / carob bean gum is the ground and purified galactomannan from carob seeds. It is a plant-derived hydrocolloid used to manage texture and water in foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Collected or extracted from carob tree seeds, then cleaned, milled and/or purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: A high-molecular-weight carbohydrate rather than a simple sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for thickening, stabilising or controlling texture.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Tara gum is a galactomannan obtained from tara seeds.
entries.expanded_summary: Tara gum is a galactomannan obtained from tara seeds. It is a plant-derived hydrocolloid used to manage texture and water in foods.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Collected or extracted from seeds of the tara tree, then cleaned, milled and/or purified to food-grade specifications.
entries.fact_1_copy: A high-molecular-weight carbohydrate rather than a simple sugar.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for thickening, stabilising or controlling texture.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Polysorbate 20 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and lauric acid.
entries.expanded_summary: Polysorbate 20 is an emulsifier made from sorbitol-derived material, polyoxyethylene chains and lauric acid. Its molecular design gives it both water-friendly and fat-friendly parts.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by esterifying sorbitol/sorbitan with fatty acids and adding polyoxyethylene chains through controlled chemical processing.
entries.fact_1_copy: Helps oils, fats and water stay mixed and can stabilise foams or dispersions.
entries.fact_2_copy: The fatty-acid feedstock may come from plant or animal fats, while the final emulsifier is chemically processed.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Sucrose acetate isobutyrate (SAIB) is a dense, oil-soluble sucrose ester used mainly to keep flavour oils evenly suspended in drinks.
entries.expanded_summary: Sucrose acetate isobutyrate (SAIB) is a dense, oil-soluble sucrose ester used mainly to keep flavour oils evenly suspended in drinks.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by esterifying sucrose with acetic and isobutyric acid derivatives, producing a heavy, viscous liquid.
entries.fact_1_copy: Acts as a weighting or stabilising agent in beverage emulsions.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its density helps stop citrus and other flavour oils floating to the top of a drink.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium polyaspartate is a negatively charged polymer built from aspartic-acid units.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium polyaspartate is a negatively charged polymer built from aspartic-acid units. It is used mainly to help prevent potassium bitartrate crystals forming in wine.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by polymerising aspartic-acid-derived material and converting the polymer to its potassium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Aspartic acid is an amino acid; the additive is a manufactured polymer of that building block.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a stabiliser against tartrate crystal formation in wine.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium carboxymethylcellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium carboxymethylcellulose is a chemically modified form of plant cellulose. Introducing carboxymethyl groups, then conversion to the sodium salt changes cellulose from an insoluble plant fibre into a material with useful thickening, film-forming or stabilising behaviour.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with purified plant cellulose, which is reacted under controlled conditions to introduce carboxymethyl groups, then conversion to the sodium salt; the product is then washed and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant cellulose, commonly from wood pulp or cotton-derived material.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as a thickener, stabiliser, film former or texture modifier depending on the derivative.
entries.evidence_copy: Europe's food-safety authority found that modified celluloses including 466 are not absorbed intact, are not fermented and are excreted in faeces. It found no evidence of gene damage, did not consider a numerical daily limit necessary for the general population and reported no safety concern at current uses. The review also considered the available studies about emulsifiers, so findings about a different emulsifier should not automatically be applied to 466.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Follow-up re-evaluation of sodium carboxymethylcellulose E466 (2022)

entries.consumer_display_name: Diacetyltartaric and fatty acid esters of glycerol
entries.entry_title: Diacetyltartaric and fatty acid esters of glycerol (472e)
entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Diacetyltartaric and fatty acid esters of glycerol are emulsifiers made by adding diacetyltartaric acid-derived groups to mono- and diglyceride-type fat molecules.
entries.expanded_summary: Diacetyltartaric and fatty acid esters of glycerol are emulsifiers made by adding diacetyltartaric acid-derived groups to mono- and diglyceride-type fat molecules. The modification changes how the molecules interact with dough, fat and water.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made from glycerol/fatty-acid materials plus diacetyltartaric acid-derived components through controlled esterification; fatty-acid sources can be plant or animal.
entries.fact_1_copy: Built on glycerol and fatty acids, the same broad building blocks found in edible fats.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used as emulsifiers and texture/process aids, with some forms particularly important in bakery applications.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Dioctyl sodium sulphosuccinate is a synthetic surfactant.
entries.expanded_summary: Dioctyl sodium sulphosuccinate is a synthetic surfactant. Its molecule has both water-attracting and fat-attracting regions, allowing it to reduce surface tension and improve wetting or dispersion.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by esterification and sulphonation reactions followed by conversion to the sodium salt and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a wetting, dispersing or emulsifying agent in specific applications.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Potassium bicarbonate / potassium carbonate are inorganic carbonate salts.
entries.expanded_summary: Potassium bicarbonate / potassium carbonate are inorganic carbonate salts. These are the potassium counterparts of sodium bicarbonate/carbonate.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured from purified mineral or chemical starting materials by reacting carbon dioxide/carbonate chemistry with a potassium-containing base or salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Depending on the form, used for raising, acidity control, anticaking or processing.
entries.fact_2_copy: Carbonates and bicarbonates change pH and can release carbon dioxide under acidic or heated conditions.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Ammonium chloride is an inorganic ammonium salt with a distinctly salty, slightly sharp taste.
entries.expanded_summary: Ammonium chloride is an inorganic ammonium salt with a distinctly salty, slightly sharp taste.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced industrially from ammonia and hydrochloric acid or recovered from related chemical processes.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used for acidity control, dough/yeast processing or characteristic flavour in some foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Magnesium sulphate is the mineral salt also known as Epsom salt.
entries.expanded_summary: Magnesium sulphate is the mineral salt also known as Epsom salt.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from mineral/brine sources or manufactured and crystallised to food-grade purity.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as a mineral salt, firming/coagulating aid or processing ingredient.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Magnesium oxide, also known as magnesia, is an inorganic alkaline material.
entries.expanded_summary: Magnesium oxide, also known as magnesia, is an inorganic alkaline material. It is a basic mineral oxide used for pH adjustment, anticaking and magnesium-related processing functions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Made by calcining magnesium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide from mineral/brine sources.
entries.fact_1_copy: A strongly or moderately basic magnesium-containing compound used for processing rather than flavour.
entries.fact_2_copy: Its technical name can sound severe because concentrated material is reactive; food use is controlled and application-specific.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium silicate is an inorganic calcium-silicate powder.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium silicate is an inorganic calcium-silicate powder.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by reacting calcium and silica sources under controlled conditions.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used mainly as an anticaking agent and carrier.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Aluminium silicate is an inorganic clay/silicate material.
entries.expanded_summary: Aluminium silicate is an inorganic clay/silicate material.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Obtained from mineral sources or produced as a purified precipitated silicate.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used as an anticaking or processing material.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Calcium gluconate is the calcium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose.
entries.expanded_summary: Calcium gluconate is the calcium salt of gluconic acid, an acid made by oxidising glucose. The gluconate part is highly water-compatible and can bind minerals.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from fermentation/oxidation-derived gluconic acid followed by neutralisation with a calcium-containing source.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glucose-derived gluconic acid.
entries.fact_2_copy: Depending on the mineral, used for mineral delivery, acidity control, sequestration, colour stabilisation or processing.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Monopotassium L-glutamate is the potassium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste.
entries.expanded_summary: Monopotassium L-glutamate is the potassium salt of glutamic acid, the amino acid associated with umami taste. It belongs to the same glutamate flavour-enhancer family as MSG.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Glutamic acid is commonly produced by microbial fermentation of sugars or starch hydrolysates, then neutralised with a potassium source to make the salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Glutamate occurs naturally in foods including tomatoes, mushrooms, seaweed and aged cheeses.
entries.fact_2_copy: The glutamate ion provides savoury umami taste.
entries.fact_3_copy: Added glutamate and naturally occurring glutamate are the same glutamate ion once dissolved in food.

entries.source_profile_definition: Microorganisms such as bacteria, yeasts or fungi are grown in controlled tanks and fed sugars or other nutrients. They make the target substance as they grow. The liquid or culture is then filtered or separated, and the additive is concentrated and purified. The finished additive normally does not contain live production microbes.
entries.tile_summary: Disodium 5′-ribonucleotides is a flavour-enhancing mixture containing the nucleotide salts disodium guanylate and disodium inosinate.
entries.expanded_summary: Disodium 5′-ribonucleotides is a flavour-enhancing mixture containing the nucleotide salts disodium guanylate and disodium inosinate. It is designed to intensify savoury umami taste.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced from purified nucleotide materials, commonly via fermentation/enzymatic routes, then blended in controlled proportions as sodium salts.
entries.fact_1_copy: A mixture rather than one single molecule — principally E627 and E631 chemistry.
entries.fact_2_copy: Particularly effective alongside glutamate/MSG.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used in savoury seasonings, snacks, soups and similar products.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with animal or insect material. The target substance is separated from that material and then cleaned, refined or converted into a stable food-grade form.
entries.tile_summary: Beeswax is the natural wax secreted by honeybees to build honeycomb.
entries.expanded_summary: Beeswax is the natural wax secreted by honeybees to build honeycomb. Food-grade white or yellow beeswax is purified and used mainly as a coating or glazing material.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Collected from honeycomb wax and refined by melting, filtration and, for white beeswax, further bleaching/purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Produced by honeybees.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to create protective or glossy coatings and to control moisture transfer.
entries.fact_3_copy: Its animal origin may matter for vegan or other ingredient preferences.

entries.source_profile_definition: A purified gas used in or around food. It may dissolve into the product, displace oxygen in a package, create bubbles or foam, or act as a propellant.
entries.tile_summary: Nitrogen is an inert gas that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.
entries.expanded_summary: Nitrogen is an inert gas that makes up about 78% of Earth's atmosphere.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Separated and purified from air, then compressed or liquefied.
entries.fact_1_copy: Used to displace oxygen, protect food from oxidation, create packaging atmospheres or provide pressure.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used for its gas/pressure properties rather than as a conventional solid or liquid ingredient.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener.
entries.expanded_summary: Acesulphame potassium (acesulfame K) is a high-intensity synthetic sweetener. Its molecule contains a cyclic sulphamate structure and provides sweetness with very little mass compared with sugar.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by multi-step chemical synthesis and converted to the potassium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: Roughly 200 times sweeter than sucrose, depending on the food matrix.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used to provide sweetness with little added energy and is often blended with other sweeteners.
entries.fact_3_copy: Blending can reduce aftertaste and produce a sweetness profile closer to sugar.
entries.evidence_copy: A 2025 European review concluded that intake of 950 was unlikely to be associated with cancer, disrupted glucose or insulin control, cardiovascular disease or organ toxicity. It set a daily safety limit of 15 milligrams per kilogram of body weight and found that high-exposure estimates were generally below it. The review separately recommended a tighter limit for one manufacturing impurity, distinguishing product-purity control from the safety conclusion on the sweetener itself.
entries.evidence_source_1_link_label: European food-safety authority: Re-evaluation of acesulfame K E950 (2025)

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with plant or seaweed material. The useful colour, gum, wax or other component is separated from the raw material, then concentrated, refined or purified for food use.
entries.tile_summary: Thaumatin is an intensely sweet protein obtained from the West African katemfe fruit.
entries.expanded_summary: Thaumatin is an intensely sweet protein obtained from the West African katemfe fruit. Unlike most high-intensity sweeteners, its sweetness comes from a protein rather than a small molecule.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Extracted and purified from the arils of Thaumatococcus daniellii fruit.
entries.fact_1_copy: Katemfe fruit from Thaumatococcus daniellii.
entries.fact_2_copy: Extremely sweet by weight and also used to modify or enhance flavour.

entries.source_profile_definition: The same additive identity can legitimately be made from different starting materials or by different manufacturing routes. The additive code alone therefore cannot tell you one reliable origin.
entries.tile_summary: Xylitol is a five-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and vegetables.
entries.expanded_summary: Xylitol is a five-carbon sugar alcohol that occurs naturally in small amounts in fruits and vegetables. It has sweetness close to sucrose and produces a noticeable cooling sensation in the mouth.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial xylitol is commonly made by hydrogenating xylose obtained from plant hemicellulose; fermentation routes also exist.
entries.fact_1_copy: Industrial xylose can come from wood, corn cobs and other plant fibre streams.
entries.fact_2_copy: Dissolving xylitol absorbs heat, creating the cooling effect familiar in sugar-free gum.
entries.fact_3_copy: Used as a bulk sweetener, particularly in confectionery and oral-care-style foods.

entries.source_profile_definition: A protein that performs a specific biological job. Food enzymes may be extracted from plants or animals, or produced by microorganisms grown by fermentation. They speed up reactions such as breaking starch, protein or fat into smaller components.
entries.tile_summary: Glucose oxidase is an enzyme that converts glucose and oxygen into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide.
entries.expanded_summary: Glucose oxidase is an enzyme that converts glucose and oxygen into gluconic acid and hydrogen peroxide. Food manufacturers use that reaction to remove oxygen or alter dough and preservation conditions.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Commercial preparations are commonly produced by fermentation with selected fungi or other microorganisms, then filtered and purified.
entries.fact_1_copy: Uses oxygen while oxidising glucose.
entries.fact_2_copy: Can strengthen dough, reduce oxygen in packaged systems or support preservation-related processing.
entries.fact_3_copy: A protein enzyme rather than a synthetic preservative molecule.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Acid-treated starch is starch whose long chains have been partially broken down by acid treatment.
entries.expanded_summary: Acid-treated starch is starch whose long chains have been partially broken down by acid treatment. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes controlled acid hydrolysis, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Distarch phosphate is starch chains cross-linked to one another with phosphate bridges.
entries.expanded_summary: Distarch phosphate is starch chains cross-linked to one another with phosphate bridges. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes phosphate cross-linking, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Starts with a natural material such as starch, cellulose, fat, sugar, gum or resin. It is deliberately changed using methods such as acid or alkali treatment, enzymes, heat, oxidation, or by attaching small chemical groups so it behaves differently in food — for instance to thicken better, stay stable after freezing or help oil and water stay mixed.
entries.tile_summary: Hydroxypropyl distarch phosphate is phosphate-cross-linked starch with hydroxypropyl groups.
entries.expanded_summary: Hydroxypropyl distarch phosphate is phosphate-cross-linked starch with hydroxypropyl groups. The starting material is ordinary food starch, but it is deliberately modified so it performs more reliably during heating, freezing, mixing or storage.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Starts with plant starch — commonly maize, potato, tapioca, wheat or another approved source — and undergoes cross-linking plus hydroxypropylation, followed by washing and purification.
entries.fact_1_copy: Plant starch.
entries.fact_2_copy: Native starch can break down, thin out or retrograde under processing; modification tunes stability, viscosity, emulsification or freeze-thaw behaviour.
entries.fact_3_copy: The additive number identifies the modification, not the crop from which the starch was made.

entries.source_profile_definition: Built from simpler starting chemicals through one or more controlled chemical reactions, then separated and purified to a defined food-grade composition. The starting chemicals may themselves come from petroleum, minerals, plants or other industrial sources; the substance-specific description should say when a notable origin is known.
entries.tile_summary: Polyethylene glycol 8000 is a high-molecular-weight water-soluble polymer made from repeating ethylene oxide units.
entries.expanded_summary: Polyethylene glycol 8000 is a high-molecular-weight water-soluble polymer made from repeating ethylene oxide units. The '8000' refers to its approximate molecular-weight range, not an additive code.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Produced by controlled polymerisation of ethylene oxide and purified to a defined molecular-weight distribution.
entries.fact_1_copy: A polyethylene glycol polymer, not polyethylene plastic.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used in specialised coating, carrier or processing applications where its waxy, water-soluble properties are useful.

entries.source_profile_definition: Includes minerals and simple salts, acids, bases, oxides and related compounds. Some are refined directly from mineral deposits; others are made by reacting basic mineral-derived or industrial starting materials and then purified.
entries.tile_summary: Sodium hydrosulphite, also called sodium dithionite, is a strong inorganic reducing agent.
entries.expanded_summary: Sodium hydrosulphite, also called sodium dithionite, is a strong inorganic reducing agent. In food processing it is used for specialised bleaching or redox-control applications rather than as a general-purpose preservative.
entries.source_preparation_copy: Manufactured by controlled reduction of sulphur-containing inorganic compounds and crystallised as the sodium salt.
entries.fact_1_copy: A powerful reducing agent — the chemical opposite of an oxidising agent.
entries.fact_2_copy: Used only in specific processing applications where reduction or bleaching is required.
entries.fact_3_copy: FSANZ lists this additive by name without a numeric additive code.
